transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

I guess what finally pushed me to come in is… I don’t feel like myself in this really quiet, flattened way. It’s not exactly that something dramatic happened, which almost makes it harder to explain. It’s more like the part of me that used to naturally reach for people, or feel interested in things, or get some pleasure from my day, has sort of gone dim.

I work in mental health and substance abuse social work, so I’m used to being engaged with people and meaning and all of that, and I can still do what I’m supposed to do, mostly. I show up. I answer emails. I get through obligations. But it feels like I’m just moving from one requirement to the next without that usual spark or pull toward anything.

And outside of work, things I used to really care about—yoga, going to galleries, journaling, even just wanting to connect with friends—none of it feels like it reaches me the same way. I’ll think, “I should do that, that used to help,” and then it’s like there’s no internal motion behind it. I’m not exactly choosing to withdraw, but I’m also not reaching out. Everything just feels very quiet inside.
How long have you been feeling this flattened, low-motivation way—days, weeks, or longer?

Longer. I’d say it’s been about eight months now, which feels strange to say out loud because I think for a while I kept framing it as just an adjustment period.

It really started after we took my older relative into our apartment. At first I thought, okay, this is a big household change, of course I’m tired, of course my routines are disrupted. But the change in me—how I’m thinking, how I’m working, how I’m connecting or not connecting with people—has just sort of continued. It hasn’t been like a bad week and then it lifts. It’s been this steady dulling for most of those eight months.
Besides feeling flat and unmotivated, have you noticed any changes in your sleep, appetite, or energy levels over these past eight months?

I don’t know that I can give a very clean answer to that, honestly. I haven’t been tracking it closely enough to say, like, “my sleep changed exactly this way” or “my appetite is definitely different.” It’s all kind of blended together with the general flatness.

Energy-wise… I mean, I feel less internally driven, but I don’t know if that’s the same as being physically tired. I can still get through the day and do the basics, so I haven’t thought of it as a clear energy problem. Sleep and appetite haven’t jumped out at me as the main thing, if that makes sense. It’s more that nothing feels like it pulls me forward.
Have you noticed any feelings of worthlessness, excessive guilt, or thoughts about death or hurting yourself during this time?

I don’t know… I wouldn’t say that’s been the main thing. I haven’t really been walking around thinking, “I’m worthless,” exactly, or feeling some huge guilt about something specific.

There’s definitely a kind of self-criticism that comes with not functioning the way I’m used to—like, I’ll notice myself not reaching out, not doing the things I know are good for me, and then I can get frustrated with myself. But it doesn’t feel like this intense guilt or like I believe I’m a bad person. It’s more confusion and disappointment, maybe.

As far as death or hurting myself… no, I haven’t really noticed that. I mean, I’ve had moments of wanting everything to just pause, or wanting to not have to keep explaining myself, but not in the sense of wanting to die or planning to hurt myself. It’s more like I feel muted, not actively self-destructive.

Have you been diagnosed with any new medical conditions, started any new medications, or noticed any physical symptoms like headaches, dizziness, or changes in your thinking or memory over these past eight months?

I don’t think so—not in any clear way that I could point to. I haven’t had some new diagnosis come up, and I haven’t started some new medication where I’d say, “Oh, that’s when everything shifted.”

And physically, nothing has really stood out to me like, you know, persistent headaches or dizziness or something that made me think there was a separate medical issue happening. I’m trying to be careful because I know sometimes you don’t notice things until someone asks, but I don’t have a specific symptom like that to report.

Thinking and memory… I mean, I sometimes feel less sharp because I’m less engaged, but I don’t know that I’d describe it as a memory problem exactly. It’s more like I’m not as plugged in. But no, nothing obvious or new that I’ve noticed medically.
Focusing just on sleep—over these past eight months, have you noticed any change in how easily you fall asleep, how often you wake during the night, or what time you wake up in the morning?

Sleep specifically… I’m not sure I can say there’s been a clear pattern. I’ve thought about it because I know it’s one of those things people ask about, but I don’t have a strong before-and-after comparison in my mind.

I don’t think I’ve had a dramatic change in falling asleep, like lying awake for hours every night or anything I could confidently point to. And I don’t really remember waking up repeatedly in the night in some new way. Morning wake-up time is a little harder to answer, because my schedule and motivation have felt kind of blurred together, so sometimes I’m just slower to get going, but I’m not sure that means I’m waking earlier or later.

So… I’d say I haven’t noticed a definite sleep change. If there is one, it hasn’t been obvious enough that I’ve been tracking it.
Over these past eight months, have you noticed it's harder to concentrate, focus on tasks, or make decisions—at work or elsewhere—compared to before?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed a clear change there, honestly. I mean, there are times when I feel less “locked in,” if that makes sense, but it’s hard for me to separate whether that’s actual concentration being worse or just me not being as engaged with things.

At work or with tasks, I don’t think I’ve suddenly been unable to focus or make decisions in a way that stands out sharply compared to before. I can still think things through. Sometimes I may take longer to get started or I overthink whether I’m approaching something the right way, but I wouldn’t say I’ve had a definite, obvious decline in concentration or decision-making.

So I guess my answer is… not really, or at least not in a way I can confidently point to as a new problem over these eight months.

Over these eight months, does this flat, low feeling stay pretty much the same every day regardless of what's happening, or does it seem to ease up on days when things with your relative's care are calmer and worsen when that stress increases?

It’s… it’s not completely tied to the day-to-day stress, I don’t think. I mean, caring for my relative definitely takes something out of me, and when that situation is more demanding I can feel more drained or preoccupied. But the thing that finally made me come in is that even when there’s a calmer day, when nothing particularly urgent is happening, I still don’t really feel like myself.

It’s like the part of me that used to naturally reach toward people has gone very quiet. I used to get something back from work, from being with clients, from feeling useful, and now I’m mostly just doing what I’m supposed to do. Same with things that used to feel like mine—yoga, going to galleries, even journaling. I can still know those are things I value, but I don’t feel pulled toward them in the same way. It’s more like I’m moving through obligations than actually taking pleasure in them.

So yes, stress can make it heavier, but the flatness doesn’t really lift just because the caregiving day is easier. That’s what worries me.

Over these past eight months, would you say this flat, low-interest feeling has been present nearly every day, most of the day, or does it noticeably come and go depending on what's happening that day?

It’s been there pretty much all the time, I think. I don’t want to overstate it like every single minute of every single day is exactly the same, because there are moments where I’m distracted or I can function and do what needs doing. But the overall feeling—the flatness, the not really reaching toward anything—that’s been there nearly every day.

It doesn’t feel like it comes and goes based on one good or bad day. That’s part of what finally made me come in. It’s like the part of me that used to naturally want to connect with people, or take pleasure in my work, or feel pulled toward yoga, galleries, journaling… that part has gone very quiet. I still know those things matter to me, and I can still go through the motions, but it feels more like I’m moving through obligations than actually wanting or enjoying them.

So yes, I’d say it’s present most days, and for a lot of the day. It’s just sort of the background now.

Before your relative moved in about eight months ago, would you say your mood and interest in things were genuinely different—like your usual baseline self—or have you had stretches of feeling this same kind of low, flat, unmotivated way at other points earlier in your life?

Before my relative moved in, I do think I was more like myself. Not perfect, I mean, I’ve had stressful periods like anyone, especially with work being emotionally demanding, but I still felt… connected to things. I could have a hard week and still look forward to a yoga class, or want to go see an exhibit, or sit down and journal because it helped me feel grounded.

And with work, even when it was tiring, I used to get something back from it. I felt engaged with people, with clients, with the sense that I was useful. I also used to reach out more naturally—text people, make plans, feel curious about what was going on with them. It didn’t feel like I had to force every bit of it.

This past eight months feels different from that. What finally brought me in is that it’s like that part of me has gone very quiet—the part that reaches for people and takes pleasure in work, yoga, galleries, even journaling. I’m still doing a lot of what I’m supposed to do, but it feels more like I’m moving through obligations than actually wanting things or enjoying them.

I don’t really remember another stretch earlier in my life that felt exactly like this, not in this persistent, flat way.
Over these past eight months, have you noticed any change in your appetite or in your weight, either an increase or a decrease?

I’m not really sure, to be honest. I haven’t been tracking it in any careful way. My appetite feels… maybe kind of variable, but I can’t say there’s been a clear increase or decrease that I’ve noticed.

My weight—I don’t weigh myself regularly, so I don’t have a number to give you. My clothes don’t feel dramatically different or anything like that. I suppose with the way things have been, meals can get a little irregular just because the day gets away from me, but I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed a definite weight change.

It feels tied to when my older relative moved into our apartment, yes. I mean, I can’t say it was like a switch flipped on that exact day, but when I look back, that’s really when this whole change started becoming noticeable.

It’s been about eight months now, and over that time I’ve felt different in the way I think, the way I work, and the way I connect—or don’t connect—with people. Before that, I felt more like myself. Since then, it’s like everything has gradually gotten flatter and harder to reach for.

So, yes, in my mind the timing is connected to that change at home. That’s sort of the marker I keep coming back to when I try to explain when this began.

It’s been about eight months altogether. I keep measuring it from when we took my older relative into our apartment, because that’s when I started noticing this shift in myself.

It wasn’t just one isolated bad week or something that came and went. It’s been this whole ongoing change in how I’m thinking, how I’m functioning at work, and how I connect with people. I feel like I’ve been saying “about eight months” a lot, but that really is the clearest way I can place it.

I wish I could say there are breaks where it really lifts, but… not substantially, no. Even when I’m technically away from the caregiving part or I have a little time to myself, I don’t feel like I snap back into being who I used to be.

That’s actually a big part of why I came in. It’s not just that I’m tired or stressed in the moment. It’s more like the part of me that used to naturally reach for people, or get something out of my work, or want to go to yoga, or wander through a gallery, or even sit and journal—it’s gone very quiet. I can still make myself do certain obligations, and I do, but it feels like I’m mostly moving through them rather than actually being engaged or nourished by them.

So even if there’s a day where I’m not actively dealing with things at home, I don’t really feel like my old self comes back. It’s more like the same flatness is still there in the background.

I think that’s really what finally pushed me to come in, honestly. It isn’t just that I’m busy or tired or that I have less free time. It’s that the part of me that used to sort of naturally reach outward—toward people, toward my work, toward things I cared about—has gotten very quiet.

I used to get something from my work, even when it was hard. I used to want to go to yoga, or go look at galleries, or sit and journal and feel like I was processing things. And now I can still do obligations, I can still show up for things if I have to, but it feels like I’m mostly just moving through them. There’s not much pleasure or pull there.

So, no, even during breaks, I don’t really feel like my old self comes back. That’s the part that scares me a little.

Have people close to you—family, friends, or coworkers—commented that you seem to be moving, speaking, or reacting more slowly than usual, or alternatively that you seem more restless or fidgety than before?

A few people have noticed something, yes, though I don’t think they’ve framed it exactly as me moving slowly or being restless. It’s more like… they notice these odd little moments where I’m not quite acting like myself.

In team meetings, for example, I’ve caught myself arranging pens in these really exact patterns on the table—like lining them up by color or angle, and then adjusting them over and over until they feel right. And I’ll realize people have gone quiet or someone is watching me, and I feel embarrassed because I wasn’t fully aware I’d drifted into doing it.

It’s happened with clients too, which bothers me more. A person will say something, and before I can stop myself I’ll repeat a phrase they just said, almost under my breath or sometimes out loud enough that they notice. Not in a reflective listening way, like professionally, but just… echoing it. And then there’s this look people give me, like I’ve stepped outside the room for a second.

So I don’t know if that counts as slower or fidgetier, exactly. But yes, people have reacted to me seeming off, or like I’m not quite tracking in the usual way.

During those moments—arranging the pens or repeating a client's words—do you feel like you're aware of doing it in the moment but almost stuck or on autopilot, or does it feel more like you completely lose track of time and only realize afterward what happened?

It’s more like I’m partly aware, but not quickly enough to stop it, if that makes sense. I don’t think I completely black out or lose a chunk of time. It’s not like I come to and wonder where I’ve been.

With the pens, for example, I’ll be in a team meeting and I’m still hearing people, at least on some level, but then I notice my hands have started lining them up in these very exact little patterns—by color, or making the angles match, or spacing them evenly. And then I’ll adjust one, and then another, and it becomes this loop where it feels strangely hard to just leave them alone. I’m aware enough to feel embarrassed when I realize someone is watching, but it also feels like I was on autopilot for the first part of it.

With clients, the repeating is worse because it feels less voluntary. Someone says a phrase, and before I’ve really decided to say anything, I hear myself repeat part of it. Sometimes it’s quiet, but sometimes it’s loud enough that they notice. And then there’s this pause, like the room changes, and I realize I’ve done something odd. I don’t feel like I’ve lost time exactly—it’s more like I stepped a little outside of the normal rhythm of the conversation and then suddenly I’m back in it, trying to cover for it.

Aside from the pen-arranging and repeating words, have you or others noticed times when you become completely still or rigid for a while, hold unusual postures, or go mute and unresponsive for stretches of time?

Not really in the way you’re describing, no. I don’t think I’ve had periods where I’m completely frozen or rigid, or where I’m mute and people can’t get a response from me for a long stretch.

What I have noticed is more those smaller, strange moments I mentioned—like in meetings, I’ll start arranging pens into these exact little patterns, lining them up and correcting the spacing, and I don’t seem able to just let it be right away. Or with clients, I’ll repeat a phrase they just said before I’ve really chosen to speak. It’s not that I’m totally unresponsive, exactly. I’m still there, but it feels like I slip out of the normal flow for a moment, and then I come back and notice people looking at me like something odd just happened.

So, no, not completely still or mute for stretches. More like these brief episodes where my behavior gets… odd or mechanical, and other people pick up on it before I fully do.

Have you or anyone else noticed times when you resist simple requests or someone trying to reposition you—like pushing back against being moved—or alternatively when your arm or body stays in a position someone placed it in, as if it were stuck there?

No, I don’t think I’ve had that specific thing—like someone tries to move my arm and I push back, or my body stays posed where they put it. That doesn’t really sound like what’s been happening.

It’s more… the things people notice are these odd, brief behaviors. Like I’ve said, in team meetings I’ll start arranging pens into these very exact patterns—spacing them, lining them up, fixing the angles—and I can get sort of caught in it before I fully realize I’m doing it. Or with clients, I’ll repeat a phrase they just said, almost automatically, before I can stop myself. And then people look at me strangely, like I’ve stepped outside the room for a second.

But being physically repositioned or stuck in a posture—no, I can’t think of that happening.
Have you noticed anything unusual lately, like hearing sounds or voices others don't seem to hear, or having thoughts or beliefs that others have told you seem out of the ordinary or hard to explain?

Yes… I mean, not so much voices, at least not in the way people usually mean that. But I have been having this thing at work that I know is going to sound hard to explain.

I’ve started feeling pretty convinced that certain comments in staff emails are not just normal comments. Like someone will write something very ordinary about “documentation being reviewed” or “keeping an eye on patterns,” and I know logically that could apply to everyone, but it feels like it’s aimed at me specifically. Like there’s a second meaning underneath it, and I’m supposed to pick up on it.

And it’s not just emails. Sometimes people pause outside my office, or I hear them stop talking when they get near my door, and I get this strong feeling that it’s connected to me—that they’re watching me or evaluating how I’m doing. My supervisor has told me that’s not happening, that it’s just routine workplace stuff, and I try to take that in, I really do. But the reassurance doesn’t really settle it. It keeps coming back as this feeling that there’s something being signaled, like I’m missing the official explanation but understanding the real one.

I know saying it out loud makes it sound unlikely. I’m aware of that. But in the moment it feels very real, and it’s been hard to shake.

target_item.reason: The question is asking about observable changes in movement, speech, or reactions, which most directly relates to abnormal/disorganized behavior and motor control.

patient.answer:
A few people have noticed something, yes, though I don’t think they’ve framed it exactly as me moving slowly or being restless. It’s more like… they notice these odd little moments where I’m not quite acting like myself.

In team meetings, for example, I’ve caught myself arranging pens in these really exact patterns on the table—like lining them up by color or angle, and then adjusting them over and over until they feel right. And I’ll realize people have gone quiet or someone is watching me, and I feel embarrassed because I wasn’t fully aware I’d drifted into doing it.

It’s happened with clients too, which bothers me more. A person will say something, and before I can stop myself I’ll repeat a phrase they just said, almost under my breath or sometimes out loud enough that they notice. Not in a reflective listening way, like professionally, but just… echoing it. And then there’s this look people give me, like I’ve stepped outside the room for a second.

So I don’t know if that counts as slower or fidgetier, exactly. But yes, people have reacted to me seeming off, or like I’m not quite tracking in the usual way.

doctor.intent: Clarify the nature of the pen-arranging and phrase-echoing episodes—specifically whether the patient experiences any loss of awareness, 'blanking out,' or time gaps during these moments (suggesting dissociation) versus feeling driven by an urge they can't resist (suggesting compulsion) versus simply drifting into repetitive motor/verbal patterns without any felt urge (suggesting catatonic-like features)
doctor.question: During those moments—arranging the pens or repeating a client's words—do you feel like you're aware of doing it in the moment but almost stuck or on autopilot, or does it feel more like you completely lose track of time and only realize afterward what happened?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: A few times in team meetings or even with clients, I’ve caught myself arranging pens in these exact patterns or repeating a phrase someone just said before I can stop myself, and people look at me like I’ve stepped outside the room somehow.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's awareness and experience during the pen-arranging and phrase-repeating episodes, which directly concerns the abnormal or disorganized behaviors described in this symptom item.

patient.answer:
It’s more like I’m partly aware, but not quickly enough to stop it, if that makes sense. I don’t think I completely black out or lose a chunk of time. It’s not like I come to and wonder where I’ve been.

With the pens, for example, I’ll be in a team meeting and I’m still hearing people, at least on some level, but then I notice my hands have started lining them up in these very exact little patterns—by color, or making the angles match, or spacing them evenly. And then I’ll adjust one, and then another, and it becomes this loop where it feels strangely hard to just leave them alone. I’m aware enough to feel embarrassed when I realize someone is watching, but it also feels like I was on autopilot for the first part of it.

With clients, the repeating is worse because it feels less voluntary. Someone says a phrase, and before I’ve really decided to say anything, I hear myself repeat part of it. Sometimes it’s quiet, but sometimes it’s loud enough that they notice. And then there’s this pause, like the room changes, and I realize I’ve done something odd. I don’t feel like I’ve lost time exactly—it’s more like I stepped a little outside of the normal rhythm of the conversation and then suddenly I’m back in it, trying to cover for it.

doctor.intent: Assess for additional catatonic signs (e.g., posturing, waxy flexibility, prolonged immobility, or mutism) to determine whether the echolalia and stereotyped pen-arranging reflect a catatonic syndrome accompanying the depressive episode
doctor.question: Aside from the pen-arranging and repeating words, have you or others noticed times when you become completely still or rigid for a while, hold unusual postures, or go mute and unresponsive for stretches of time?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: A few times in team meetings or even with clients, I’ve caught myself arranging pens in these exact patterns or repeating a phrase someone just said before I can stop myself, and people look at me like I’ve stepped outside the room somehow.
target_item.reason: The question asks about catatonic-like motor or behavioral abnormalities such as rigidity, unusual postures, mutism, and unresponsiveness, which falls under disorganized or abnormal behavior.

patient.answer:
Not really in the way you’re describing, no. I don’t think I’ve had periods where I’m completely frozen or rigid, or where I’m mute and people can’t get a response from me for a long stretch.

What I have noticed is more those smaller, strange moments I mentioned—like in meetings, I’ll start arranging pens into these exact little patterns, lining them up and correcting the spacing, and I don’t seem able to just let it be right away. Or with clients, I’ll repeat a phrase they just said before I’ve really chosen to speak. It’s not that I’m totally unresponsive, exactly. I’m still there, but it feels like I slip out of the normal flow for a moment, and then I come back and notice people looking at me like something odd just happened.

So, no, not completely still or mute for stretches. More like these brief episodes where my behavior gets… odd or mechanical, and other people pick up on it before I fully do.

doctor.intent: Assess for additional catatonic signs (negativism or waxy flexibility) to determine if criteria for catatonia are met, which would change the diagnostic and treatment approach
doctor.question: Have you or anyone else noticed times when you resist simple requests or someone trying to reposition you—like pushing back against being moved—or alternatively when your arm or body stays in a position someone placed it in, as if it were stuck there?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: A few times in team meetings or even with clients, I’ve caught myself arranging pens in these exact patterns or repeating a phrase someone just said before I can stop myself, and people look at me like I’ve stepped outside the room somehow.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about abnormal motor behavior/catatonic-like signs such as resisting movement or maintaining imposed postures, which falls under disturbed behavior and motor control.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think I’ve had that specific thing—like someone tries to move my arm and I push back, or my body stays posed where they put it. That doesn’t really sound like what’s been happening.

It’s more… the things people notice are these odd, brief behaviors. Like I’ve said, in team meetings I’ll start arranging pens into these very exact patterns—spacing them, lining them up, fixing the angles—and I can get sort of caught in it before I fully realize I’m doing it. Or with clients, I’ll repeat a phrase they just said, almost automatically, before I can stop myself. And then people look at me strangely, like I’ve stepped outside the room for a second.

But being physically repositioned or stuck in a posture—no, I can’t think of that happening.

doctor.intent: Screen for psychotic symptoms (hallucinations or unusual beliefs) that might explain the catatonic-like behaviors and flattened affect, to distinguish depression with catatonic features from a primary psychotic disorder
doctor.question: Have you noticed anything unusual lately, like hearing sounds or voices others don't seem to hear, or having thoughts or beliefs that others have told you seem out of the ordinary or hard to explain?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds unlikely, but I’ve become convinced that certain comments in staff emails and even the way people pause outside my office are meant to signal that I’m being watched or evaluated, and reassurance from my supervisor hasn’t really shaken that feeling.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychotic experiences, especially unusual thoughts or beliefs; the matching profile item is delusions about emails and hallway pauses signaling that she is being watched or evaluated.

patient.answer:
Yes… I mean, not so much voices, at least not in the way people usually mean that. But I have been having this thing at work that I know is going to sound hard to explain.

I’ve started feeling pretty convinced that certain comments in staff emails are not just normal comments. Like someone will write something very ordinary about “documentation being reviewed” or “keeping an eye on patterns,” and I know logically that could apply to everyone, but it feels like it’s aimed at me specifically. Like there’s a second meaning underneath it, and I’m supposed to pick up on it.

And it’s not just emails. Sometimes people pause outside my office, or I hear them stop talking when they get near my door, and I get this strong feeling that it’s connected to me—that they’re watching me or evaluating how I’m doing. My supervisor has told me that’s not happening, that it’s just routine workplace stuff, and I try to take that in, I really do. But the reassurance doesn’t really settle it. It keeps coming back as this feeling that there’s something being signaled, like I’m missing the official explanation but understanding the real one.

I know saying it out loud makes it sound unlikely. I’m aware of that. But in the moment it feels very real, and it’s been hard to shake.

inference.note: Added psychotic features (referential/persecutory delusions about work emails and being watched) and catatonic-like behaviors (stereotyped pen-arranging, echolalia-like repeating of clients' words) on top of the pre-existing 8-month non-reactive anhedonic/flat mood syndrome. This shifts the differential from a pure depressive/adjustment picture toward severe depression with psychotic and catatonic features (F32.3), schizoaffective disorder depressive type (F25.1), or a catatonia syndrome possibly secondary to an underlying mood/medical process (F06.1), while ruling out simple adjustment disorder or uncomplicated MDD without psychotic features given the clear delusional content and motor stereotypies.
